sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Much of my 2010 challenge came true, via Brussels
sections.para: My December 2010 IBWAS keynote in Lisbon set out five focuses and twelve actions, from ethical hacking to software liability, and called Portugal the possible Switzerland of hacking. Sixteen years on, much came true through slow EU regulation rather than fear. The Portugal part, an ethical security industry, is still mostly to do.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Twelve actions, many achieved through regulation, not through fear
sections.para: The 2010 keynote had 168 slides, five focuses and twelve actions, and argued software deserves health-and-safety respect. Portugal, with nothing to lose, could be the Switzerland of hacking. More came true than expected, mostly from Brussels, but the mechanism was a decade of law, not fear.

sections.label: The talk
sections.line: Bold ideas proposed; the press took up one line
sections.para: On 17 December 2010 I gave the IBWAS'10 keynote at ISCTE in Lisbon, opening with a disclaimer that it was personal opinion. The press picked up Portugal as the Switzerland of hacking. The deck had four movements: five focuses and twelve actions, fear, Portuguese website examples, and a challenge to Portugal.

sections.label: Five focuses
sections.line: All five focuses still stand, especially security as intelligence
sections.para: The focuses were respect for software, application security as business intelligence and competitive advantage, a working security market, and OWASP as an enabler. Security as business intelligence anticipated today's argument that GenAI's value is understanding reality. A working market remains weakest, since buyers still cannot tell secure software from insecure.

sections.label: Twelve actions
sections.line: Liability, disclosure and SSL arrived; score cards did not
sections.para: Software falls under strict EU product liability from 9 December 2026, ENISA has run a vulnerability database since May 2025, and the Cyber Resilience Act requires 24-hour reporting of exploited vulnerabilities. Portugal's Decreto-Lei 125/2025 applies from 3 April 2026, and HTTPS passed 50%. Score cards, insurance and open-source funding did not happen.

sections.label: The fear section
sections.line: The health-and-safety analogy held; the fear mechanism did not
sections.para: The middle of the deck was deliberately scary, asking how many people must die before application security was taken seriously and proposing a day-long internet fire drill. The comparison with water, food and cars was right. But governments moved through a decade of slow regulation, liability and reporting duties, not a single disaster.

sections.label: The challenge to Portugal
sections.line: Small countries can lead a sector; Portugal has not
sections.para: The talk called Portugal depressed and argued an open, ethical security industry could help, costing only courage, focus and commitment. The core idea, that a small country can choose a sector and lead, returned in Judo for small countries. Portugal changed, but did not become the Switzerland of hacking.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: No causal claim; the commentary is written now
sections.para: The EU's laws have their own long history, so no causal claim is made. The slides are from 2010, unchanged, while the commentary is written now. The video seems to be gone, leaving the slides as the record, and attendees who remember it differently are invited to write in.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: Sources: the 2010 slides, a 2011 post, legal briefings
sections.para: Drafted from a voice memo of 16 October 2026. Sources are the slides on the OWASP wiki, a blog post of 12 January 2011, Hogan Lovells on the Product Liability Directive, the European Commission on the EUVD, McCann FitzGerald on the Cyber Resilience Act and PwC Portugal on Decreto-Lei 125/2025.
